On the day the Wang Jingwei government published, in the Zhonghua Ribao, 'The Chongqing Blue Shirts' Shanghai District Organization and Its Roster,' Gu Shenyan gave the order to burn down the whole of the Huaxing Trading Company — and, without meaning to, brought on a disaster. The fire spread downward from the top floor of the Xianghu Building and soon swallowed the entire tower. Amid the wail of the fire engines' sirens he stood a long time at a street-facing window of the New World Hotel, the flames on the far building leaping and leaping in his eyes.
Gu Shenyan turned his head slowly and said to the subordinates standing behind him with bowed heads, You must remember this day.

The day was the 28th of November, 1941. The Juntong's ten sections, eight action squads, and five intelligence groups across the Shanghai region were all blown. Gu Shenyan, on receiving the order to fall back to Chongqing, chose instead to stay. He said to Lin Nansheng, To give up Shanghai is to blind ourselves in one eye.
Lin Nansheng reminded him, with great care: To stay in Shanghai is to disobey Mr. Dai's order.

Have you ever considered why we have come to such a pass? Gu Shenyan looked at him, gave a long sigh, and went on, Once any organization makes loyalty to a man, or to some clique, its spiritual mainstay, the tragedy of today is past avoiding. For a moment Lin Nansheng did not know what to say. Gu Shenyan put on the felt hat he had been holding in his hand. He was to go, separately, to Hangzhou and to Nanjing, to recruit fresh hands. His last words to Lin Nansheng were, Your task is to wait for me to come back.

That night, when Lin Nansheng burst into the garret where Zhu Yizhen lived, he was in the uniform of the Peace Army, one arm wrapped in a bandage and slung from his neck, like a young officer slipped out of an army hospital in search of pleasure.
You haven't thrown all my clothes out, I hope? Lin Nansheng said to Zhu Yizhen with a smile. I mean to stay here a few days.
Zhu Yizhen could not smile. The whole evening she had sat at the embroidery table reading that copy of the Zhonghua Ribao, and now she let her gaze come to rest on Lin Nansheng's slung arm.

It is nothing. Still smiling, Lin Nansheng pulled the bandage off with a careless hand and, glancing round at the four walls, said, This is more like a home now than it was at first. Zhu Yizhen still would not speak. She took out a set of pajamas that had been left in the cupboard and laid them on the bed, then turned and sat down at the embroidery table, breathed on her hands, stiff with cold, took up needle and thread, and began to embroider the silk.

It was a strange night; from time to time the far wail of a siren came through the window, but inside, the room was so still that there was only the sound of thread passing through silk. Lin Nansheng lay on the bed a while, then threw off the quilt and stood barefoot on the floor. Zhu Yizhen spoke at last, for the first time, her eyes on the half-worked butterfly, and said, You ought to be getting out, not coming here.
Someone always has to stay behind. Lin Nansheng hesitated, then went over and laid both hands on her shoulders, kneading them a while like a masseur, and said, You cannot sit up until dawn.
Zhu Yizhen gently freed herself from his hands and said, One night is nothing; tomorrow I will go and buy bedding.
Lin Nansheng withdrew to the bed without a sound and said, It was wrong of me to come.
Zhu Yizhen gave a small smile and said, Sleep well.

A few days later the Japanese army took over the whole concession. From early morning the planes wheeled low, and countless leaflets came scattering down like snow; yet the streets of the Japanese quarter looked strangely deserted and clean, with only the puttee-wrapped Chinese policemen pacing in the cold wind. Toward noon Zhu Yizhen went out, but soon came back.
Japan has declared war on Britain and America. The moment she was through the door she said, a little breathless, This morning they sank the gunboat Peterel where it lay moored in the Huangpu.
With that she took off her Western dress, changed into a cheongsam, and quickly put her hair up before the mirror.
Leaning by the window, Lin Nansheng watched her quietly and said, Can you get out of Shanghai today?
Zhu Yizhen was taken aback, and said, Out or not, I have to go. As she spoke she turned and wrung out a towel, wiped the makeup from her face, and added, There is half a loaf of bread in the drawer.
As she pulled the door open Lin Nansheng stopped her and said, Let me go in your place.
Zhu Yizhen smiled and said, That is impossible.
Then let me go with you.
That too is impossible.
And if I had a way out of the city?

Zhu Yizhen said no more; she raised her eyes and looked earnestly at Lin Nansheng. But the way they walked in the street was nothing like people hurrying to get out of the city; it was more like a young officer strolling with his sweetheart. Reaching a telephone box, Lin Nansheng went in and made a call, then came out and, his arm again about Zhu Yizhen's waist, went to a sake house at the roadside.
Now and then a troop truck packed with Japanese soldiers rolled down the avenue; they were crossing Suzhou Creek into the heart of Shanghai.
Zhu Yizhen looked at the cups and dishes on the table and said, How long would you have me wait?
Lin Nansheng said nothing. He drank sip by sip and ate bite by bite, and waited until a black Nissan sedan pulled up outside the door before he set down his chopsticks, rose, and said, Let us go.

Zhu Yizhen remembered this car, and remembered too the toothbrush-mustached Japanese man in the driver's seat. But this time, once they had climbed in, the toothbrush mustache did not start the engine at once; instead he said to Lin Nansheng, in fluent Chinese, We are finished — you said we would not meet again.
Can you not do a friend one favor? Lin Nansheng said, smiling.
We are not friends. Looking at a military truck passing beyond the window, the toothbrush mustache said, I could kill the two of you right now.

Better think of it as one more piece of business. Still smiling, Lin Nansheng took out a small key and slid it from behind into the man's suit pocket, and said, There is a safe-deposit box at the Central Reserve Bank; see us out of the city and what is in it is yours.
The toothbrush mustache did not move; the right hand thrust into the inside pocket of his coat never let go of a pistol.
Lin Nansheng patted his shoulder and, still smiling, said, Kobayashi, killing a man takes courage.
Kobayashi Daisuke stared at Lin Nansheng's face in the rearview mirror a good while before he said, Lin-san, in that uniform, once you are caught you will be shot.
The smile on Lin Nansheng's face slowly froze. He closed his eyes, leaned back in the seat, and said mildly, Drive.

Kobayashi Daisuke was a second secretary at the Japanese consulate in Shanghai. From the first time he traded intelligence with Lin Nansheng, he had known that he had already lost his own country, just as he had lost his wife and child. Kobayashi Daisuke's wife and child had died in a car accident, the driver a drunken marine lieutenant. A few weeks later, on the very night the lieutenant was released in open court, he set a pistol under his own jaw — and in the end did not pull the trigger.

Well past the last checkpoint, the black Nissan pulled up at the edge of a lonely lane. Lin Nansheng said nothing; when he had seen Zhu Yizhen out of the car, he drew his pistol and pressed it to the back of Kobayashi Daisuke's neck.
You know I am not afraid to die. Laying both hands on the wheel, Kobayashi Daisuke said calmly, Life lost its meaning for me long ago.
Lin Nansheng sighed and said, Get out.

Obediently Kobayashi Daisuke got out, went to the trunk, opened it of his own accord, then turned to face the black muzzle, his eyes on Lin Nansheng, and drew out one by one everything on him that could prove his identity, dropping it all at his feet, the little key along with it. He raised his head, looked a last time at the leaden sky, and climbed into the trunk, closing his eyes as if to sleep. In the instant the shot rang out, he saw his wife and his young son.

When Zhu Yizhen ran back to the car, Lin Nansheng was crouched on the ground, gathering up one by one Kobayashi Daisuke's wallet, papers, pistol, watch, ring, and that little key, and putting them in his pocket.
What did you come back for? Lin Nansheng looked up at her and said, If it were I who had died, you would not have got away.
If he meant to kill us, he need not have waited until we were out of the city.
He would have done it sooner or later. With that Lin Nansheng stood, put the little key into Zhu Yizhen's hand, and said, Keep it safe — it is the key to your drawer.

Zhu Yizhen understood at once that there had never been any safe-deposit box at the bank — that he was now only an intelligence agent at the end of his rope. After a moment's hesitation she opened the passenger door, got in, looked at Lin Nansheng's ever-paler face, and said, You had no need to help me like this.
It is not to help you. Lin Nansheng turned his head to the bare fields and said, I do it for myself.

At nightfall they parted before a ruined temple at a fork of two roads. Zhu Yizhen went to find her organization and pass on intelligence; Lin Nansheng drove to the dyke along the Taipu River, where a thin, scattered snow began to fall out of the night sky. He opened the trunk, went carefully over the body, then took Kobayashi Daisuke's wallet, papers, pistol, watch, and ring from his own pocket and threw them one by one into the river. Last of all he slipped the car out of gear and heaved it into the water.

Tired and hungry, Lin Nansheng got back to the ruined temple deep in the night, but Zhu Yizhen was not waiting inside. Only toward noon the next day did she come walking up the path from far off, a bundle over her arm, her overcoat and cheongsam changed now for a short padded jacket.
Zhu Yizhen handed Lin Nansheng the bundle; inside were two pieces of rice cake and a man's padded jacket. Eat, and then change, she said; those clothes of yours draw far too much notice.

That night, on their way back to Shanghai, they put up at an inn, and like a couple long married they washed in silence and went to bed in silence. In six years it was the first time they had lain side by side under one quilt, each of them careful — careful even later, when they made love. They held their breath as best they could. Afterward Lin Nansheng said in her ear, Tell me — how have you lived these six years?
Zhu Yizhen did not speak. In the darkness she clenched her teeth hard, until Lin Nansheng pried them apart with his tongue, and then she breathed one long breath into his mouth.
At dawn the next day Zhu Yizhen said suddenly, I have a husband.
Lin Nansheng's eyes went wide, but he soon found the answer in hers, and said, But he is already dead.
